scope: USA empirical studies plus explicitly labeled Australian suburban comparator

studies.citation: Spurlock, C. A., Todd-Blick, A., Wong-Parodi, G., & Walker, V. (2020). Children, Income, and the Impact of Home Delivery on Household Shopping Trips. Transportation Research Record, 2674(10), 335–350.
studies.data_period: WholeTraveler, Bay Area nine counties, spring 2018; 1,012 usable respondents from 60,000 mailed invitations.
studies.treatment_or_exposure: Reported deliveries and respondent-stated additional trips absent those deliveries; not an opening treatment.
studies.outcomes: Vehicle/nonvehicle shopping trips; substituted versus supplemental purchases.
studies.identification: Multinomial logit, household-clustered errors; stated counterfactual, no exogenous adoption.
studies.reading_status: Publisher full HTML methods read; abstract and selected findings read; full results tables not audited.
studies.read_pages_or_sections: HTML Data, Survey, Model sections; abstract.
studies.annotation: Home delivery is associated with both substitution and additional consumption. The survey asks about actual purchases in the preceding week and what respondents would have done without delivery. Authors report that deliveries replace approximately 12% of vehicle shopping trips, while approximately 9% of delivered purchases supplement consumption. These have different denominators and cannot be subtracted into a net trip effect. Four product groups and household circumstances matter. The design does not establish that opening a delivery point caused a change in travel. The 1.74% survey response, English-only online questionnaire and affluent, educated sample constrain representativeness. These are pre-COVID observations; therefore mixed effects are not solely a pandemic artefact.
studies.transfer_to_russia: Ask goods-specific counterfactuals and distinguish no purchase, separate trip, and chained trip. Do not assume one parcel equals one saved centre visit.

studies.citation: Xu, L., & Saphores, J.-D. (2024). Does e-shopping impact household travel? Evidence from the 2017 U.S. NHTS. Journal of Transport Geography, 115, 103827.
studies.data_period: 2017 NHTS, travel days April 2016–April 2017; starting dataset 129,696 households; this is not the final matched sample size.
studies.treatment_or_exposure: Online delivered orders per household member in past 30 days: ≤1 baseline, (1,4], >4. Not delivery-point availability.
studies.outcomes: Trips, miles, VMT, shopping proportions; bounds for shared household trips.
studies.identification: Propensity score matching on observables; conditional exchangeability required; residual balance worse on weekends.
studies.reading_status: Publisher cached full methods and results sections actually read via web; PDF unavailable (403). Not claiming whole-paper reading.
studies.annotation: Higher e-shopping is associated with more travel in several groups. Among medium-frequency households in low-density areas, matched weekday differences scaled to a month are about eight additional trips and 104 miles, including 31 shopping miles. High-frequency dense-area weekend differences are statistically indistinguishable from zero. The study treats households jointly and brackets counts where members might shop together. It separates weekday and weekend travel and matches groups within density bands. Monthly estimates scale a single travel day; they are not observed monthly diaries. Propensity matching addresses measured selection rather than unobserved preferences or residential self-selection. It cannot identify the effect of a new pickup point or prove that online shopping expands rural autonomy.
studies.transfer_to_russia: Density and car access are moderators; preserve household joint travel and avoid extrapolating one-day diary estimates without sensitivity analysis.

studies.citation: Shah, H., Carrel, A. L., & Le, H. T. K. (2024; online 2022). Impacts of teleworking and online shopping on travel: a tour-based analysis. Transportation.
studies.data_period: 2019 Puget Sound survey, April–June; 801 people originally, final 545 people/470 households with one-week diaries.
studies.unit: Individual, weekly aggregation of home-based tours.
studies.treatment_or_exposure: Online shopping latent factor: time online and days receiving packages/other deliveries; telework duration separately.
studies.outcomes: Mandatory, maintenance and discretionary tours: trips, travel time, chained VMT share.
studies.identification: Cross-sectional SEM, robust ML, bootstrap indirect effects; no causal opening design.
studies.reading_status: Full original PMC HTML downloaded; actual methods, results Tables 1–4 and interpretation read.
studies.read_pages_or_sections: HTML Data processing, Model specification, Results; Tables 1–4.
studies.annotation: This pre-pandemic study finds no statistically significant relationship between online shopping and maintenance or discretionary tours. Estimated standardized paths are 0.014 (SE 0.076) and −0.037 (SE 0.065), respectively. Teleworking instead reduces mandatory and maintenance tours and changes shopping indirectly through commuting. Weekly diaries preserve trip chains that one-day trip counts can miss. The authors also compare pseudo one-day diaries to demonstrate sensitivity to observation windows. The final sample excludes 143 respondents with neither online shopping nor telework and does not model interactions within the household, limiting population inference. Delivery measures count days with deliveries, not parcels. The SEM paths express an assumed activity structure, not randomized causal effects.
studies.transfer_to_russia: Measure complete trip chains and commuting. A disappearing shopping stop need not remove a whole trip. Keep null effects as a pre-specified possibility.

studies.citation: Ranjbari, A., Diehl, C., Dalla Chiara, G., & Goodchild, A. (2023). Do parcel lockers reduce delivery times? Evidence from the field. Transportation Research Part E, 172, 103070.
studies.data_period: Seattle Belltown, pre/post 2020–2021; 116 package-delivery observations; two nearby condominium towers.
studies.unit: Courier delivery observation, treated building versus control building.
studies.treatment_or_exposure: Installation of common-carrier residential lobby locker; not Amazon-exclusive and not staffed public PVZ.
studies.outcomes: Courier time inside building, curb vehicle dwell; resident satisfaction separately.
studies.identification: Nonrandom before/after control DiD; OLS/WLS/Gamma; only two buildings and different seasons.
studies.reading_status: Full PDF saved; methods, results and limitations actually read.
studies.annotation: A residential common-carrier locker changes courier operations rather than directly measuring shoppers’ trips. The controlled field comparison finds a 33% reduction in curb dwell under OLS, but it is not statistically significant (p=0.275). Results for time inside the building depend on model choice: OLS is insignificant while weighted/Gamma specifications suggest larger reductions, with significance sensitive to volume controls. Accordingly, “lockers significantly reduce all delivery time” overstates the evidence. Observations cover two high-rise buildings during the pandemic; restrictions, seasonality and sample size limit inference. This is a dense urban lobby service, not suburban public collection infrastructure. It supplies no estimate of retail closures, population growth or the extent of a settlement’s functional area.
studies.transfer_to_russia: Keep courier operations separate from consumer accessibility and regional hierarchy. Pre-specify primary outcomes and report insignificant results and model dependence.

studies.citation: Leung, A., Lachapelle, U., & Burke, M. (2023). Spatio-temporal analysis of Australia Post parcel locker use during the initial system growth phase in Queensland (2013–2017). Journal of Transport Geography, 110, 103634.
studies.country: Australia — explicit car-oriented suburban comparator, not USA
studies.data_period: Australia Post Queensland transaction records, 2013–2017; 51 lockers; 904,280 parcels/391,626 collections. Address-linkage records have different denominators.
studies.unit: Locker-day; anonymized residential address–registered locker pair.
studies.treatment_or_exposure: Network growth and locker location typology (central, suburban, outer metropolitan, regional).
studies.outcomes: Collection timing/volume; parcel dwell; network distance between registered home and chosen locker.
studies.identification: Descriptive OD/network analysis, OLS with clustered errors and mixed effects; not causal rollout evaluation.
studies.reading_status: Full PDF saved; methods, results, limitations actually read.
studies.annotation: Actual transaction data reveal different rhythms in central and suburban locations and substantial use outside business hours. The residential-address to chosen-locker network-distance median is 3.35 km, but the mean is 23.07 km because of a long tail. Some users register several lockers, including central locations farther from home. This undermines a purely nearest-point catchment assumption. Residential street numbers were removed, so origins are approximated by street midpoints. Truncated identifiers require deduplication; transaction and address-linkage denominators must not be mixed. The data do not observe actual collection travel, mode, replaced shopping trips or staffed collection points. The paper’s abstract labels a dwell statistic in minutes, while the methods/results use hours; avoid propagating this unit inconsistency. Administrative data are not publicly shareable.
studies.transfer_to_russia: Estimate observed origin–destination catchments where possible; compare with travel-time accessibility scenarios instead of declaring Voronoi cells functional areas.

studies.citation: Chava, S., Oettl, A., Singh, M., & Zeng, L. (2024). Creative Destruction? Impact of E-Commerce on the Retail Sector. Management Science, 70(4), 2168–2187.
studies.data_period: READ VERSION: NBER WP30077 May2022, doi10.3386/w30077. Worker/QCEW 2010–2016; NETS stores2010–2014; 39 post2009 FC shocks; 2.6m workers/57 firms and 3.2m stores.
studies.treatment_or_exposure: Major e-retailer fulfillment-center openings; local e-commerce proxy, not public pickup-point adoption.
studies.outcomes: Retail worker income/hours, store sales/employment/exit, sector job growth; neighboring counties.
studies.identification: Staggered DiD/event study, worker/store FE, matching, firm-time and region-time FE, sector triple differences; supplementary USPS-distance × subsidies IV needs exclusion argument.
studies.reading_status: Full NBER PDF saved; methods/data/results actually read. Journal metadata verified; final journal estimates not re-audited.
studies.read_pages_or_sections: PDF pp.6–16 methods/data; pp.17–25 and28–32 results (printed pages differ by2).
studies.annotation: The working paper links fulfillment-center rollout to lower local traditional retail sales and hourly earnings, with heterogeneous store responses and effects extending to nearby counties. Small and young stores are more prone to exit, while larger stores adjust employment. Earnings effects largely disappear beyond 100 miles in the paper’s ring analysis. Warehouse employment gains are geographically concentrated, so retail losses and logistics benefits need not accrue to the same places. Rich fixed effects and pre-trend diagnostics improve credibility but do not make warehouse siting random. Subsidies and postal-network proximity can affect local outcomes through other channels; the supplementary instrument cannot be imported uncritically. These are pre-COVID data and the saved text is the 2022 working-paper version, not the 2024 final article.
studies.transfer_to_russia: Separate recipient settlements from warehouse-host job shocks. Include neighboring-centre outcomes and spatial exposure; never use already exposed neighbors as untreated controls.

studies.citation: Chung, J. (2023). The spillover effect of E-commerce on local retail real estate markets. Regional Science and Urban Economics, 101, 103919.
studies.data_period: Journal: US retail property transactions2007–2017; FC openings2010–2014. Author’s2021 Atlanta Fed account instead uses2013–2015 openings; versions must remain distinct.
studies.unit: Retail property transaction and county labor indicators.
studies.treatment_or_exposure: Amazon fulfillment-center opening, not locker or consumer-PVZ access.
studies.outcomes: Retail property value; transport/warehousing employment, wages and establishments.
studies.identification: Matched county DiD; property/market controls; spatial heterogeneity in likely worker residence.
studies.reading_status: Publisher abstract plus methods/results section snippets read; full author Atlanta Fed exposition read. Journal full PDF not obtained.
studies.read_pages_or_sections: Journal Data and methodology/Baseline results snippets; full2021 author exposition, no journal page claim.
studies.annotation: Contrary to a uniform retail decline narrative, the journal reports a 5.2% premium for retail property in counties receiving a fulfillment center; the effect emerges in year two and lasts through year five. Transport and warehousing employment and wages rise, and impacts are stronger where warehouse workers likely live. This is evidence consistent with an income channel, not proof that delivery access benefits every small settlement. Transaction prices can move differently from retail employment or consumer travel. County aggregation combines the warehouse-host economy with surrounding retail markets. The earlier author exposition has a different entry window and cannot silently substitute for the journal specification. Matched trends do not resolve every siting confound.
studies.transfer_to_russia: Estimate distinct outcomes and geographic recipients: property value, shops, employment, mobility and population need not share signs. Warehouse-host effects are a separate treatment.

studies.citation: Mookerjee, U. (2026). Impact of e-commerce on local retail markets: evidence from Amazon fulfillment centers. Empirical Economics, 70(2).
studies.data_period: County labor outcomes2010–2017; journal2026, DOIyear2025. Exact final sample not verified.
studies.unit: County and retail worker skill groups.
studies.treatment_or_exposure: Amazon fulfillment-center presence/openings, not pickup-point access.
studies.outcomes: Total retail employment and skill composition; wage distribution.
studies.identification: Two-stage event study with staggered adoption stated in abstract; detailed estimator/control construction not verified.
studies.reading_status: Journal abstract only; downloaded2021 dissertation is a distinct unreviewed background version and not evidence of reading journal methods.
studies.read_pages_or_sections: Abstract only; no journal page claim.
studies.annotation: The journal abstract reports little overall change in retail employment alongside rising high-skilled and falling low-skilled employment. Distributional adjustment can therefore be hidden by an aggregate null. It proposes competition from online purchases followed by adaptation through firms selling on platforms. The mechanism and detailed design have not been independently audited here because full journal access was unavailable. Its fulfillment-center exposure bundles labor-demand, logistics and consumer-market channels. The result does not directly contradict a negative store-level or low-skill effect, and cannot be treated as a causal estimate for Russian pickup-point openings. The saved dissertation is older and must not be substituted for the journal’s two-stage event-study evidence.
studies.transfer_to_russia: Pre-specify totals and composition; a null population or employment total does not imply no local restructuring.
